article.title: Messages that fail with an error code
article.excerpt: A failed status always carries a reason. The first question is which layer wrote it — the platform or the provider.

p: A failure is either the platform refusing the request before it left, or the provider refusing it after. The code tells you which, and therefore who owns the fix.

head: Code
Layer
Typical cause
rows: Bad parameter, key bound to no channel, no ACTIVE channel, messageType not recognized
messageId not found, or belongs to another tenant
Submission rate exceeded — back off and retry
The provider's own refusal, kept verbatim so you can match it against their documentation

steps.p: It is the provider's own wording, so it matches their docs and support answers directly.
A message that unexpectedly jumped encoding can be refused for length. A wide-encoding segment budget is much smaller than a GSM one.
A number the provider has not approved for that route is refused per message, even on an ACTIVE connection.
If only one provider is refusing, the log's channel comparison tells you immediately — and routing can move traffic off it while you investigate.

sections.note: A provider refusal is not billed, which is a useful signal: a message with a null providerMessageId never became an accepted send on the provider side.

sections.h: Platform refusals are the easy ones
p: A 40000 on every call usually means a binding problem rather than a payload problem — most often a key that was never bound to a channel, or a connection that is no longer ACTIVE. Both are console fixes, not code changes.
